content:
This episode resonated with me a lot, so I’m taking some notes.
How to View Work # In the workplace, we’re not looking for Mr. Right, and we can’t find Mr. Right. There will inevitably be some things that don’t sit well with us.
But how the current boss and company are is their own issue. Don’t try to change “corporate culture.” Bryan compares corporate culture to “marinade”—individuals entering it will only be assimilated, and even the boss themselves may not be able to change the corporate culture. If you don’t agree with the culture, just leave.
We should focus our attention on ourselves, treat ourselves as an independent company, and engage in B2B cooperation with the current company, focusing on getting what we want—whether it’s skills, money, status, connections, reputation, etc.
We should constantly ask ourselves: “What do I want to become in one year, two years, five years…?” After figuring that out, work backwards to determine what we should be doing now.
Before joining a company, you can do two things:
Assume each job will only last two years: Two years is actually equivalent to the time it takes to get a master’s degree Maintain a “goal list”: Write down everything you want to gain from this company in these two years If all goals have been completed and there are no new goals, that’s the time to look for the next partner.
This is actually very similar to what I’ve been practicing recently. I also have a list that records my “long-term plans for the technical department and product planning.”
This list is simply divided into:
Product-related Functional: Features I’m interested in implementing, features I think can create the most value for the company Non-functional: Such as refactoring, optimization, architecture design, etc. Development process-related: Such as optimizing development speed, avoiding technical debt accumulation, etc. In my daily routine, besides regular work, I invest time in these topics.
When I find it too difficult to push forward in the company, or when I can’t do what I want to do for a long time, I might slowly consider leaving.
This doesn’t mean the company’s direction is wrong, but rather that I can’t get the skills I want.
Career Burnout # Additionally, Bryan also mentioned how he overcomes career burnout.
He mentioned that he records work tasks and gives them a happiness rating from -10 to +10.
Over time, you can observe what you actually like to do and recognize your talents and passions.
To eliminate burnout, you can consider two dimensions:
Vertical development: Go deeper (e.g., challenge yourself from building 10-story buildings to 30-story buildings). Horizontal expansion: Serve more people or learn extended skills (e.g., engineers learning fire safety, architectural aesthetics). However, Bryan also mentioned not to blindly change careers. He doesn’t recommend directly switching careers without a foundation (e.g., engineer to pastry chef), as this is usually just an escape from the current situation, with a very high failure rate.
The Art of Resignation # Ideal resignation should be because you see a better goal, not just because you dislike the current situation.
So recognizing what you want is still the most important thing.
Additionally, Bryan specifically mentioned not to stay because of a “salary increase to retain you.” If you stay only because the boss increased your pay, your value in the boss’s mind will become a bargaining chip that can be bought with money at any time, your chances of future promotion will be very low, and other colleagues might also look at you differently.
A healthy attitude is to thank the company cheerfully and insist on moving to the next stage of your career.
Conclusion # Thanks to Bryan and thanks to Boen for letting me hear such a great program.
Although it’s similar to my realizations this year, I couldn’t express it so systematically.
Hope this helps you who are reading this.
title: The Essence of the Workplace is Mutual Benefit

content:
This article was translated by AI. If you find any errors, please feel free to email me at jk29666338@gmail.com 🙏. This year (2025), I experienced significant career burnout.
And I wasn’t the only one.
I saw people around me developing health issues due to long-term overwork.
I saw people working hard to prepare for interviews, only to become cynical and weary in the end.
By chance, I came across this video. It tells the story of a software engineer who, from a young age, worked hard to learn new technologies and earned a good salary. However, due to reasons like the sudden passing of a colleague, his wife’s illness, and his children growing up, he ultimately volunteered to be laid off:
At the same time, I saw endless discussions on social media:
Software engineers claiming how much productivity AI has improved, how easy their life is now, and how much their working hours have decreased. Software companies introducing AI development to improve capacity. Many job descriptions explicitly requiring candidates to know how to collaborate with AI. Business leaders asserting that the AI era will eliminate those who don’t use AI. New models, tools, and protocols coming out constantly, all powerful and super useful. While AI is powerful, fundamental knowledge remains important. Even the legendary Andrej Karpathy said on X (Source):
Do we really need to roll up our sleeves? # After consuming this content, I felt conflicted.
Standing before me is a high wall named AI, a field where even experts feel they are falling behind.
And it’s not just AI itself; using AI requires fundamental knowledge as support, so I still have to catch up on other basics.
Can I choose not to learn? But everyone says it’s super important, and if I don’t learn, I’ll be replaced.
Can I actually learn it all? Do I have that much time and energy? Do I still have time to learn other things I’m interested in?
Is the best way to face this giant wave of AI really to “Roll up your sleeves to not fall behind”?
Even if I catch up in the short term, how long do I have to keep chasing? Will I burn out? Will I lose out on other aspects of life?
AI Fatigue # A Forbes article touched on this situation: 《Why ‘AI Fatigue’ Is Wearing You Down And How To Beat It》.
AI Fatigue is defined as employees and organizations feeling exhausted due to the explosive growth of AI tools, excessive pressure for change, lack of support, and fear of unemployment.
The article clearly mentions five key causes of AI Fatigue:
Rapid pace of change: Frequent updates leave employees no time to master existing tools.
Lack of appropriate support and training: Companies often just give orders without providing enough resources to help employees transition.
Lack of job security: Employees learn AI sometimes not for efficiency, but out of a survival instinct.
Opaque internal communication: Leadership fails to explain the specific reasons for introducing AI, leading employees to view it as an extra burden.
Unrealistic expectations: Media and upper management mythologize AI, leading to disappointment when tools don’t yield immediate results.
I resonate deeply with this. In fact, I learned AI simply because of “3. Lack of job security,” not out of curiosity, efficiency, or encountering real problems.
And the hype on social media gave me “5. Unrealistic expectations,” thinking AI is already so powerful that it doesn’t need humans, and I might be replaced next month.
But the fact is: it’s not that powerful yet.
What is my strategy? # Project Based Learning (PBL) # I strongly agree with a conclusion in the Forbes article:
Instead of trying to understand AI technology comprehensively, concentrate on practical applications that solve real problems in your work.
We don’t actually need to spend time learning things we won’t use. Focus on solving the immediate problem first, and if you have time, try to see if AI can make the process of solving that problem better.
For example, I use Cursor, Antigravity, Gemini, and ChatGPT, and I have tried developing some small AI applications.
But I won’t go out of my way to study terms like Sub-agent, A2A, or MCP. The reason is simple: I don’t have a need for them.
Take MCP for example. In my work context, manual copy-pasting versus a model calling a tool to find information makes almost no difference in efficiency. The model might even find the wrong thing. So why should I spend a lot of time researching how to configure it, authorize it, etc.?
Faced with these new terms, I usually just get a general overview so I can pull it out if I need it later.
Some might say: “You don’t know how good it is because you haven’t used it. If you try it, you might love it.” True, but I have the following reasons:
Let the bullets fly for a while: Sometimes new technologies are just hype, not to mention flash-in-the-pan tech (like Prompt Engineering). Many things we don’t need to solve ourselves; maybe someone will build a service for us to use (possibly even for free). Productivity improvements don’t have to be instant: If something is truly good, I will eventually know about it. I can use it when it becomes a household name; I don’t need to be the first to try everything. Actually, it’s not just AI. I tend to lean towards PBL for learning any knowledge now. Set a practical problem first, then extend research directly from that issue.
Same as Ever # The book Same as Ever mentions:
Change is exciting and surprising, so it captures our attention. But behaviors that never change are history’s most powerful lessons because they preview what is to come, mirroring your future and everyone else’s future. No matter who you are, where you are from, how old you are, or how much money you make, human behavior contains timeless lessons, and this is the most important thing you can learn.
This concept is simple but easily overlooked. Once you grasp it, you can better understand your life, understand why the world looks the way it does, and face the future more comfortably.
Things that never change are important because you can know with confidence how they will shape the future. Bezos said you can’t imagine future Amazon customers not wanting low prices or fast delivery, so he could invest heavily in those things.
I find this very suitable for dealing with this increasingly fast-changing era.
Instead of focusing on “what is changing,” it is better to focus on mastering the things that do not change.
Conclusion # In this era of rapid technological change, feeling anxious is human nature. But we don’t need to drift with the tide, nor do we need to force ourselves to become experts in every new tool. Through Project Based Learning, we can return learning to needs itself, making every investment meaningful. At the same time, don’t forget to focus on those “Same as Ever” things; they are the foundation for us to settle down in this changing world.
I hope this article gives you a little strength if you are also feeling anxious. Let us go further, at our own pace.
title: Facing Information Anxiety in the AI Era: My Survival Guide with Project Based Learning

Following community conventions has many benefits, and I’ve been feeling this quite strongly recently.
I once saw a company’s error handling mechanism that seemed to be forcefully implemented by a manager after referencing some language, but it was unclear which one.
The result was that it was very difficult to use, and even the manager couldn’t clearly explain when and how to use it.
There was talk of writing documentation and standards, but it never materialized. As a result, everyone used it inconsistently, and refactoring became very troublesome.
Using community conventions avoids this problem. Besides the benefits mentioned in the article, it also saves a lot of educational costs.
If newcomers really don’t know how, they can definitely find resources and standards online.
Of course, community conventions will have limitations under special conditions, but for organizations, I think in the long run it’s better than creating your own clever tricks.

This article was translated by AI. If you find any errors, please feel free to email me at jk29666338@gmail.com 🙏. I was recently discussing an issue with a colleague about the priority of our monitoring system.
We’ve always had monitoring in place, but we haven’t been using this tool effectively, which led to this discussion.
During the discussion, we came up with two reasons for “why we shouldn’t optimize monitoring right now,” which I found interesting and reminded me of some memories, so I wanted to write an article to record them.
However, we were just evaluating, so we naturally analyzed from both positive and negative perspectives.
But for the sake of convenience in the following narrative, I’ll position my colleague as the opposing side and myself as the agreeing side.
Discussion One # Isn’t Monitoring Itself the Most Important? # My colleague believes: What’s important about monitoring is what to do after detecting something? Can we handle it?
For example, the previous Cloudflare incident—what good is monitoring if we can only wait for it to recover?
Or if a payment service provider goes down, monitoring it won’t help at all.
My Thoughts # It’s true that there can be situations where we detect something but are powerless to act.
I think to determine whether something can be handled, we first need to know about it.
If we don’t even know something has happened, how can we determine whether we can handle it?
Furthermore, while we may be technically unable to handle something, there may be administrative actions we need to take.
For example, if Cloudflare crashes, shouldn’t we notify users? How should we notify them?
If a payment service provider crashes, shouldn’t we quickly confirm the situation with them?
Without monitoring, we can only wait for users to discover the anomaly and notify us.
We’ll always be one step behind.
Discussion Two # Monitoring Isn’t the Biggest Risk Right Now # My colleague believes that the company currently has other more serious technical issues that need to be addressed.
I can’t disclose what this issue is, but it’s related to server stability and security.
So we should focus on solving that problem first.
My Thoughts # In the book “The Same as Ever,” there’s a passage I really like:
We are very good at predicting the future, just not good at predicting surprises, and the latter is often the most important key.
What no one expects is always the biggest risk, because no one expects it, so no one prepares for it; because no one prepares for it, when it appears, the damage will be magnified.
Human abilities are ultimately limited. No matter how hard we try, we cannot predict all situations.
I agree that the issue my colleague raised is very important, but since we already know about it, I don’t think it’s the real risk.
As another quote from the book mentions:
If you only prepare for foreseeable risks, then you’ll be completely unprepared for everything you don’t see
Regardless of the actual preparations we’ve made for this issue, even if we haven’t done anything yet, at least we’ve made mental preparations.
But those unimaginable things are what prevent us from even making mental preparations. And if we can detect them early, we can gain valuable preparation and response time. I believe that for these real risks, even a small time difference is precious.
Technically, how do we detect those unimaginable things as early as possible? I think it’s through monitoring.
Although we can’t monitor all data, monitoring at least ensures that no matter what happens, we can find out as quickly as possible.
title: The Biggest Risk is Always What No One Expected

content:
This article was translated by AI. If you find any errors, please feel free to email me at jk29666338@gmail.com 🙏. Result # Skip the suspense—here are the numbers first:
CI average before (last 5 runs): 12 minutes 20 seconds CI average after (last 3 runs): 7 minutes 3 seconds Improvement: 42.84%
Why I Did This # We’ve always had a CI pipeline that runs unit tests and checks for outdated packages before merges.
Recently, some team changes made the CI wait feel painful. For example, when frontend needs backend APIs, the backend branch has to merge first—and even if the code is ready, we still wait for CI. Sometimes CI fails and we debug and rerun, adding more wait time. The larger the team, the worse the delays.
We hit a short “off-season,” so I pitched my manager on optimizing CI.
Resource Check # Before touching code, I took stock:
Current CI runtime: ~11–13 minutes I had at most 3 days to work on this task, so the sooner I could finish, the better. I had zero experience with GitLab CI With that, I set some principles:
Focus on the biggest and easiest wins; skip anything requiring deep GitLab CI knowledge for now. Aim for a 50% reduction in CI time. CI Analysis # Job Timeline # To speed things up, I needed to know where time was spent. I reviewed the last two CI runs and summarized the stages (times are representative):
Stage Job 1 Job 2 Preparing the “docker” executor 14 13 Preparing environment 0 0 Getting source from Git repository 8 8 Restoring cache 10 11 Executing “step_script” stage of the job script 593 686 Saving cache for successful job 48 36 Cleaning up project directory and file based variables 1 0 Total duration* 11 minutes 17 seconds 12 minutes 38 seconds *Total duration uses the GitLab Pipeline “Duration,” so there may be slight differences from summing the numbers.
Clearly, the bottleneck is Executing “step_script” stage of the job script. That’s where we should focus.
Main Bottleneck # I dug into the Executing “step_script” stage to see what it actually does (AI-generated outline below):
Phase Command What it does Security checks sudo composer self-update --2 Upgrade Composer to v2 for compatibility and security. composer config --global audit.abandoned report Set Composer to report abandoned packages. composer audit Scan composer.json dependencies for known vulnerabilities. Install deps composer install --prefer-dist... Install PHP backend deps with faster flags (no progress bar, non-interactive). yarn install Install frontend JS deps. DB setup sudo apt-get install -y mysql-client Install MySQL client for running SQL. mysql ... CREATE DATABASE... Create two test DBs: testing and testing_sub. mysql ... CREATE USER... Create DB user user. mysql ... GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES... Grant full privileges on the test DBs. mysql ... < mysql_sub-schema.sql Import schema into testing_sub. Laravel env setup cp .env.testing.example .env Copy env template. php artisan key:generate Generate app key. php artisan config:cache Cache config. php artisan migrate --seed Run migrations and seed test data. Run tests ./vendor/phpunit/phpunit/phpunit... Run PHPUnit; pipe errors to stderr. yarn test Run frontend tests (Jest/Vitest). Not every step had timings, so I singled out the biggest chunk: PHPUnit tests.
Job 1 Job 2 PHPUnit time 09:06.684 10:34.911 Stage total 593 sec 686 sec CI total 11 minutes 17 seconds 12 minutes 38 seconds Share of stage time 92.1% 92.6% Share of job time 80.6% 83.6% PHPUnit is the primary target.
Why Is PHPUnit Slow? # Locally, most test methods finish under 0.1s, but some are abnormally slow:
Feature Test 3 and 4 are wildly slow, and Feature Test 2 has a 6s case. A “mere” 6 seconds locally can balloon on GitLab runners. I finish locally in ~130s vs. ~600s on CI—a >4x difference. The 6s+ tests became my top targets; anything under 6s wasn’t prioritized due to time limits.
Optimization in Practice # Let’s see what made those tests so slow.
Feature Test 3 # Structure overview:
<?php class FeatureTest3 { use WithFaker, RefreshDatabase; public function warmUpCache() { // Build data and store in cache } public function setUp() { parent::setUp(); // Clear cache // withoutMiddleware // Seeder } public function testFunction3() { $caches = $this->warmUpCache(); // assert } public function testFunction4() { $caches = $this->warmUpCache(); // assert } public function testFunction5() { $caches = $this->warmUpCache(); // assert } public function testFunction6() { $caches = $this->warmUpCache(); // assert } public function testFunction7() { $caches = $this->warmUpCache(); // assert } } The function under test reads from a cache DB. During tests, we build data via factories, store in DB, then cache—done in warmUpCache(). Because of complex business logic, warmUpCache() builds a lot of data and is slow. Optimizing it directly is hard within time limits, so I looked at reducing how often it runs:
Data comes from cache, not DB. Each test method is independent. So refreshing DB, seeding, clearing cache, and rebuilding cache for every test is wasteful. I added a cache reuse mechanism:
<?php class FeatureTest3 { use WithFaker, RefreshDatabase; protected static array $warmedUpCaches = []; public function warmUpCache() { // If already warmed and Redis still has the cache, reuse it if (isset(self::$warmedUpCaches[$group]) && $redis->exists($cacheVersionKey)) { $cacheVersion = $redis->get($cacheVersionKey); return [ $cacheVersion, self::$warmedUpCaches[$group], ]; } // Build data and store in cache } public function setUp() { parent::setUp(); // Stop clearing cache; share across functions // withoutMiddleware // Seeder } } Results:
PASS Tests\Feature\FeatureTest3 ✓ ... 3.05s ✓ ... 0.18s ✓ TestFunction3 7.13s ✓ TestFunction4 6.87s ✓ TestFunction5 0.14s ✓ TestFunction6 0.13s ✓ TestFunction7 0.13s Runtime dropped from ~34s to ~17.5s—almost half. CI time fell from ~12m20s to 9m13s (over 3 minutes saved).
Note: This boosts speed but risks cross-test contamination if any test mutates cache contents. Use only when cache data is read-only or well-isolated. Two tests still exceed 6s; that’s expected due to business logic. Refresh DB and seeder repeats remain, but they weren’t the biggest pain here, and time was limited.
Feature Test 4 # Structure:
<?php class FeatureTest4 { use WithFaker, RefreshDatabase; public function setUp() { parent::setUp(); // Clear cache // withoutMiddleware // Seeder $this->warmUpSearchEngine(); } public function testFunction8() { // assert } public function testFunction9() { // assert } public function testFunction10() { // assert } public function testFunction11() { // assert } public function testFunction12() { // assert } public function warmUpSearchEngine() { // Clear search engine // Build data // Store into search engine // Sleep 5 seconds } } Looks similar to Feature Test 3—reuse trick? Unfortunately no, because the function under test depends on real DB operations; using cached-only data would break correctness. But the pain is obvious: every test calls warmUpSearchEngine(), which includes a sleep(5) to wait for async import. Shortening or removing it isn’t safe. Data setup is complex as well.
Could we reduce how often warmUpSearchEngine() runs? Yes, because tests are independent and can share identical fixture data. I collapsed the test methods into one:
<?php class FeatureTest4 { use WithFaker, RefreshDatabase; public function setUp() { parent::setUp(); // Clear cache // withoutMiddleware // Seeder $this->warmUpSearchEngine(); } public function testAll() { $this->assertFunction8(); $this->assertFunction9(); $this->assertFunction10(); $this->assertFunction11(); $this->assertFunction12(); } public function assertFunction8() { // assert } public function assertFunction9() { // assert } public function assertFunction10() { // assert } public function assertFunction11() { // assert } public function assertFunction12() { // assert } public function warmUpSearchEngine() { // Clear search engine // Build data // Store into search engine // Sleep 5 seconds } } All checks live in one test, so warmUpSearchEngine() runs once.
Results:
PASS Tests\Feature\FeatureTest4 ✓ all 11.75s Tests: 1 passed (1819 assertions) Duration: 12.02s From ~42s to ~12s—about 30s saved. CI dropped from 9m13s (after Feature Test 3) to 7m51s—another ~1.5 minutes.
Is this harder to debug? Possibly, but I accepted it because:
This function rarely changes; I haven’t touched it in 2+ years. Failures usually come from the search engine, not business logic. The company is mid-refactor; this function may be sunset soon. Given time constraints and payoff, the risk felt small.
Feature Test 2 # The slow part:
<?php public function testFunction2() { // ...snip $creators = Creator::factory()->count(301)->create(); // ...snip } Why so slow? Creator has many related records created by the factory—core business logic we can’t change right now.
Why 301 creators? The command under test fetches the first 300 rows:
<?php Creator::where(xxx) ->limit(300) ->get() I considered refactors but hit dead ends:
Skip creating data: wouldn’t test the command properly. Share creators with other functions: too complex; risks coupling tests. Then it clicked: could we drop this test? Its logic largely duplicates other tests; the only unique piece is the “limit 300.” No frontend dependency or documented business rule ties to 300. Likely just an arbitrary number. I double-checked with a senior engineer; we agreed removal was safe.
Results:
Local: 6.21s → 0s CI: 7m51s → 7m07s (about 45s saved) Wrap-Up # We cut CI from ~12.5 minutes to a little over 7 minutes.
My first CI-optimization task turned out fun and impactful. The key takeaway is “resource analysis”: know your time and skills, then hit the highest-leverage issues first. Deliver value fast—that’s critical for engineers in a fast-moving world.
Future Ideas # Things I surveyed but skipped due to lower ROI or complexity:
Split jobs: e.g., separate frontend/backend tests to run in parallel. Frontend tests take ~3s, so gains are tiny. Parallelize PHP tests: run in multiple processes. But many tests touch the DB; might get flaky (untested). Migration dump: avoid rerunning 100+ migrations by using dumps. Technical hurdles and smaller-than-expected gains, so deferred.

This article was translated by AI. If you find any errors, please feel free to email me at jk29666338@gmail.com 🙏. Recently, I had a need: I wanted to polish my resume.
However, the awkward part is that during my first two years at this company, I didn’t diligently record my work.
So, if someone asked me, “What kind of issues did you resolve at your previous company?”
I could only respond with, “Uh…”
Coincidentally, I’ve been wanting to try MCP (Model Context Protocol) for a while but never had a practical need for it. So, I decided to see if MCP could help with this.
My idea was simple: use a local MCP Client to access Jira and GitLab MCP Servers, then ask an AI to analyze the issues I’ve solved and organize them into a resume format.
Jira # Antigravity # The first one I tried was Antigravity, simply because I’ve been using it a lot lately.
Connecting Antigravity to Jira is very straightforward. In the Agent screen, select MCP Servers, choose Atlassian, and complete the OAuth authentication.
Cursor # Next, I tried Cursor. Based on my experience with Antigravity, I simply copied the configuration.
You can find Manage MCP Servers in the MCP Store, then click View Raw Config to find mcp_config.json.
Go to Cursor settings, find New MCP Server, and fill in the configuration:
{ "mcpServers": { "atlassian-mcp-server": { "command": "npx", "args": [ "-y", "mcp-remote", "https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/sse" ], "env": {} } } } GitLab # GitLab officially seems to still be testing MCP, so the setup is more complex. I had to use a community-developed one called @zereight/mcp-gitlab.
For the specific installation process, please refer to: zereight/gitlab-mcp
However, I should point out that this MCP has quite a few tools. If you’re working on important projects, I recommend turning off dangerous permissions like Create, Update, and Delete to avoid accidental triggers.
The installation for Antigravity and Cursor is similar, so I won’t go into detail.
Testing # Since it was just a test, I wrote a rather casual prompt:
I am JYu. I have been working at company xxx for n years and am preparing my resume. I need you to use Jira MCP and GitLab MCP to help me organize and analyze all the projects I've worked on during this period, so I can prepare my resume. I first tried it with Cursor, but it ran out of context immediately XD.
Then I switched to Antigravity using Planning mode + Gemini 1.5 Flash, and here is the result:
Final Result # Career Summary: JYu (Software Engineer @ xxx) # Analytical and impact-driven Software Engineer with n years of experience at xxx. Expertise in backend development (PHP/Laravel), DevOps automation, and technical security. Lead contributor to critical infrastructure and financial modules.
🚀 Key Impact Areas # 1. DevOps & Infrastructure Optimization # CI/CD Pipeline Acceleration: Directed initiatives to optimize CI/CD workflows, significantly reducing build and deployment times. Deployment Automation: Developed and integrated robust deployment scripts (deploy.sh, reload-app.sh) and automated database migration triggers to enhance system stability during releases. Server Lifecycle Management: Orchestrated server transitions and handled infrastructure updates (SRE tasks) before transitioning to backend lead roles. 2. Financial & Payment Systems # Complex Withdrawal Logic: Designed and implemented the “Creator Withdrawal System,” including automated withdrawal processing and tax-compliant exports (Withholding Tax). Payment Stability: Monitored and fixed critical payment/refund failures, ensuring high reliability for financial transactions. Architecture Refactoring: Decoupled business logic from report export modules, centralizing domain logic in Services to improve maintainability and scalability. 3. Security & Compliance # CVE Mitigation: Identified and patched security vulnerabilities, including CVE-2025-14761 (Key Commitment Issue in AWS SDK for PHP), protecting S3-based encrypted assets. Invoice & Taxation: Built systems for order invoice processing and taxation module verification, ensuring financial compliance for the platform. 4. Product & Feature Engineering # Domain Modeling: Refined product taxonomy and tagging systems to support complex content discovery. V3 Platform Transition: Contributed to the backend architecture for the next-generation creator application flow. 🛠 Technical Stack # Languages & Frameworks: PHP, Laravel, Bash. Integrations: AWS SDK (S3, Encryption), Payment Providers (Ecpay, etc.), Spout (Exporters). Tools: Jira, GitLab CI/CD, Confluence (Technical documentation/Whiteboarding). 🏆 Notable Jira/GitLab Projects # xxx project (Main Platform): Heavy focus on financial reliability and security. xxx Deploy Script: Standalone toolset for platform maintenance. CatalystV3: Next-generation platform development. Conclusion # I wonder what you think of the result? XD
Personally, I think it’s a bit subpar, but then again, I didn’t put much effort into the prompt. With the right “tuning,” it definitely feels promising.
The reason I hadn’t wanted to try MCP before was that I felt it only saved some Copy & Paste time without providing much substantial help.
In fact, using the “traditional” ChatGPT approach—manually copying relevant information to the model—often feels more efficient because it prevents the model from looking at too many unnecessary files or engaging in meaningless reasoning.
However, for scenarios like “summarizing a resume” where there is a lot of context and I don’t even know how much “relevant information” there is, MCP seems perfectly suited for the task.
Overall, it was an interesting little experiment. I probably won’t use MCP very often in the short term, but I’ll think about more suitable use cases for it.

This article was translated by AI. If you find any errors, please feel free to email me at jk29666338@gmail.com 🙏. Before we begin, I must clarify: this is not a traditional book review. I want to use this article to share my biggest realization and transformation in 2025.
Furthermore, there won’t be a Table of Contents for this post, because I don’t want you to skip around.
This year, work left me physically and mentally exhausted.
Specifically, a sense of depression and powerlessness clouded my mind. It felt like my hard work was just skipping stones—vanishing without receiving any recognition or return from anyone.
Not only that, but just when I had finally rekindled my hope, adjusted my mindset, and tried to improve—feeling like I was actually performing quite well—I was harshly denied once again.
This situation started affecting my physical health. I noticed symptoms appearing: my sleep quality plummeted, and my feelings of fatigue and burnout worsened significantly. It reached a point where I couldn’t do anything properly, which in turn affected my daily life.
I felt this was no longer just ordinary stress; I was likely stepping with one foot into a mental health crisis.
So, I hurriedly booked a counseling session and looked for some books to read, hoping to solve this problem.
One day, I took leave and forced myself to go out, finding a coffee shop near my home.
While listening to Lo-fi music and smelling the aroma of coffee, I opened The Why Are You Here Cafe (also known as The Cafe on the Edge of the World).
I actually don’t know why I chose this book that day. Perhaps a mysterious force knew what I needed most at that moment?
Honestly, the plot is quite simple, perhaps even a bit boring.
But the questions asked by the characters, and the protagonist’s self-reflection, triggered deep thought.
The book revolves around three questions:
Why are you here? Do you fear death? Are you fulfilled? I believe readers seeing this might think: These three questions look simple, what is there to think about?
But if you follow the protagonist’s train of thought and ponder deeply, you’ll discover that the answers aren’t as simple as you might think.
After closing the book, I began to think about several things, including: Why exactly do I work? What is the meaning of my work? What do I hope to gain from work?
I wrote in my notebook at the time:
How did I let my life get like this? Every morning I wake up thinking about earning money, finding a better job, learning new skills, pursuing efficiency and growth, and delivering value.
But, what is it that I actually want?
Where is the finish line?
At that moment, I recalled a video I had watched that mentioned the concept of an “Ideal Life.”
It refers to what we hope our life will look like at the very end, after all our ceaseless striving.
I tried to think about this, trying to paint a picture of my ideal life.
But honestly, I had no answer at that moment.
I tried looking up the lives of successful people, hoping to use them as a reference, but it didn’t feel like what I wanted.
I was like a person swimming in the ocean—swimming desperately, yet not even knowing where the finish line was.
That evening, I went for a run. The night breeze carried a cool humidity, and my steps and breathing achieved a wonderful synchronization.
I completely zoned out, slowly inhaling and exhaling in the darkness, focusing entirely on my body. It felt as if I was the only person moving forward in the world.
Suddenly, in a fleeting moment, a thought flashed by, like an electric current shooting from my spine to the top of my head.
An indescribable energy, like an airflow, moved through my body and finally flowed to my brain.
When my brain received that energy, it seemed to become “clear.”
The sensation was so strange I thought I was running until I fainted XD.
Even now, I don’t know exactly what that feeling was. If I had to use a word to describe it, it might be a sense of “well-being” (or bliss).
In that moment, I suddenly realized: Isn’t my current life already my ideal life?
Why do I say that?
My material desires aren’t very high. I don’t want to buy luxury goods, sports cars, famous watches, etc.
I don’t pursue frequent international travel, business class flights, fine dining for every meal, or a life of debauchery.
The life I want is actually very simple: I want to be healthy, live with my friends and family, have a dwelling where I can rest properly, and have enough food and clothing.
When I listed this out and compared it with my current life…
It’s exactly the same 😇.
Suddenly, I felt the peace of the ancient poem: “Picking chrysanthemums under the eastern fence, and leisurely seeing the southern mountain.” XD
With this realization, I discovered: The things I was pursuing before didn’t seem to be what I truly wanted.
What I was pursuing were societal expectations—expectations from bosses, parents, and teachers.
This society encourages everyone to earn more money and acquire higher status.
Brands use marketing and advertising to heighten my desires, making me want to spend money on things I don’t actually want. Yet, the more I spend, the more I need to earn.
But, can having more money really buy me an ideal life?
It seems not, because I am already living my ideal life.
Of course, if my income continues to increase, I might have better material conditions.
But ultimately, regardless of whether my income and assets are several times what they are now, my life will look pretty much like this.
With this mindset, I found that things like my supervisor’s expectations or how much money I earn suddenly didn’t seem important anymore.
After shedding these external expectations, I felt quite happy—or perhaps I should say, I felt “peaceful.”
To use Buddhist terminology, it felt like a sudden “enlightenment.”
However, I don’t think I’ve completely liberated myself from that state yet. Sometimes I still care about others’ opinions, and unconsciously want to pursue more things.
The difference is, whenever I catch myself having expectations for anything, or trying to grasp something, I remind myself: “Let it be. Everything will change, everything will disappear, and then appear again.”
Facing any person, thing, or situation, I only have three options: “Accept it,” “Leave it,” or “Change it.” All I can do is choose one and do my best.
Control my efforts, but do not expect a specific result.
But following on the heels of that is the next question: Then what is important to me? Since I am already living my ideal lifestyle, what is the meaning of my continued existence? What should I pursue?
I also suddenly realized that I feel just “okay” about the profession of software engineering. It just so happens that I have this expertise, it pays well, and I don’t despise doing it.
But is software engineering my heart’s desire? Obviously not XD.
So where should my life go from here?
In The Why Are You Here Cafe, I read that the “meaning of life” actually takes a very, very long time to explore.
So I won’t know immediately what my life’s meaning is or where my life should go.
The only thing I can do is spend time learning new things and not stand still.
In The Almanack of Naval Ravikant, it is also mentioned that everyone has their own “Specific Knowledge” (Unique Advantage). These are things that are easy for you to do, but difficult for others. Or things you can do tirelessly, forgetting to eat or sleep, while others require great “discipline” to do.
Because when you are exercising your “Specific Knowledge,” you are actually “playing,” while others are “working.” I can spend 16 hours a day playing, but no one can spend 16 hours a day working.
So in the realm of “Specific Knowledge,” no one can compete with me.
However, finding that unique advantage also requires time and experimentation XD.
So looking at this whole situation now, I really have mixed feelings.
On one hand, my efforts in the first half of the year basically went down the drain.
But on the other hand, if everything had gone smoothly and I had gotten the raise as expected, I wouldn’t have had the chance to stop and think about the meaning of my life, nor would I have encountered this book.
If that were the case, I would probably have continued to bustle about, constantly sacrificing my liver (health) to satisfy others’ expectations of me in exchange for higher rewards.
I also realized that this is the first time in my life I’ve truly stopped to rethink what I actually want and rethink what happiness is.
I wonder, seeing this, how do you feel?
Where is your finish line?
title: The Book That Changed Me Most in 2025: "The Cafe on the Edge of the World: A Story About the Meaning of Life"

This article was translated by AI. If you find any errors, please feel free to email me at jk29666338@gmail.com 🙏. There are all kinds of people in this world. There are some I try to avoid working with, and one of them is people with unfounded confidence.
What are people with unfounded confidence? Simply put, they are people whose source of confidence is a mystery to me.
For normal people, confidence might come from past successes, affirmation from others, or professional knowledge in a certain field.
Unlike confident people, people with unfounded confidence have several common characteristics:
They like to belittle other people’s methods or views. They always think their way is the best solution (when you have a hammer in your hand, everything looks like a nail). They intentionally or unintentionally drop hints about how great they are. They enjoy lecturing others. They talk confidently about things they don’t understand. (Engaging in keyboard wars online). Not everyone who fits these characteristics is necessarily a person with unfounded confidence, but they are likely close. 😂
Why do I avoid such people? # Actually, these people are not necessarily annoying all the time. The main reason I avoid them is: Risk Management.
I believe that life is an infinite game. The point is “how long can you stay in the game,” not “winning or losing in the short term.”
For example, engaging in illegal industries might seem like a way to make a lot of money in the short term, but once caught, the risk could be imprisonment, which is unsustainable in the long run.
In the workplace or partnerships, people with unfounded confidence are essentially engaging in a high-risk gamble, for the following reasons:
1. Ignoring potential “Hidden Costs” # Because these people believe their plan is the “best solution,” they often overlook details and potential pitfalls during execution, and even frequently ignore individual differences.
When a person cannot see the risks, they naturally won’t manage them.
In a project, this might manifest as choosing an extremely niche technology stack just because they like it, without considering the difficulty of future maintenance and manpower costs. Or directly forcing the collaboration style of another team onto the current team without considering product attributes and manpower allocation.
2. Inability to Course-Correct # To err is human. But the scariest thing in cooperation is not making mistakes, but being unable to correct them.
When normal people encounter setbacks, they reflect: “Did I not consider something thoroughly?”
But for people with unfounded confidence, their first reaction is often: “It must be that others didn’t cooperate well” or “There is a problem with the environment.”
Since they rarely listen to others’ suggestions, this leads to the entire team missing the golden window to cut losses when a crisis occurs, watching the train derail helplessly.
3. Excessive Communication Costs # Communicating with such people often requires you to spend 80% of your energy managing their ego and self-esteem, and only 20% on dealing with the actual work.
To make them accept an objective fact, you need to go around in a big circle to avoid touching their inexplicable self-confidence. For long-term cooperation that values efficiency, this is a huge mental drain.
Conclusion # In the workplace, we all know that “trust cures all ills.” In fact, many team problems stem from a lack of trust in each other.
And trust, to put it plainly, is a sense of predictability.
I know where the boundaries of your abilities are, I know you will ask for help instead of holding on when you encounter problems, and I know you will assess risks properly instead of rushing blindly.
But those with unfounded confidence usually bring more shock than surprise.
Life is short. To go further and more steadily, I would rather choose to walk with those who “know what they don’t know,” who are humble and cautious.

This article was translated by AI. If you find any errors, please feel free to email me at jk29666338@gmail.com 🙏. Recently, due to some circumstances, I wanted to start reading some high-quality technical books.
However, after actually trying, I found that my attention span is very low, and I easily give up reading.
Maybe it’s because I’m used to reading short content, so now I don’t have the patience for this kind of long, difficult content.
The simple way might be to force myself to calm down and read. But I couldn’t help but wonder: with so many AI learning tools available now, is it possible to use AI to help me learn this difficult content?
So I started to formulate a strategy, hoping to try it out later XD
How to read difficult books? # To talk about how to use AI for assistance, we first need to understand the normal process.
Without AI, how do you read difficult books?
After a quick survey, I saw an article: 《how to read difficult books》.
Here is a brief summary of the content that is helpful to me:
Multiple Reading Method # For difficult texts, the author proposes a “Multiple Reading Method”.
The author argues that “a book should not be read only once”, but rather through layered reading steps, from initial contact to deep analysis, to truly digest the content.
So how do you proceed with the “Multiple Reading Method”?
Phase 1: Familiarity and Marking # Don’t over-analyze during the first reading; the goal is to increase familiarity with the content.
Just read and mark interesting parts with tags or highlighters.
Phase 2: Deconstruction and Connection # Use margin notes to deconstruct the key points of the first pass.
Try to restate key concepts, draw connections between viewpoints, and even write down opposing opinions.
Phase 3: External Assistance # If the text is still obscure and difficult to understand, pause reading and turn to YouTube videos, documentaries, or Podcasts to get summaries or background knowledge, and then return to reading with new understanding.
Writing as a Learning Tool # Just like my original intention for writing this blog, the author also believes that output is key to internalizing knowledge.
The author suggests writing a 1-2 page summary or even publishing a book review after reading and marking key points.
During the reading process, you should also note down concepts you want to study further at any time; after reading, rely on previous markings rather than rereading the whole book to write a summary.
Combining with AI # Ok, now I have a preliminary concept of how to read difficult books, so how should I use AI to make this faster, more convenient, and make my learning deeper?
Here is my initial strategy:
1. Skimming Content # In the article above, the author mentioned that you can read the article completely once first, with the goal of getting familiar with the content.
So now at the end of 2025, what should be done to better achieve this goal?
I will choose to use NotebookLM to generate Chinese videos and slides for each chapter. This has several benefits:
Use AI to help me quickly find key points Chinese absorption speed is better than English, after all, Chinese is my mother tongue Watching videos and slides is more relaxing than reading text After watching the videos and slides, I will have a moderate understanding of the content, and then I can enter the second stage.
2. Detailed Reading # In this stage, I will start to read the content of the book in detail.
At this time, I will start to mark some key points and create concept cards in Heptabase so that each concept can be related.
However, if I encounter questions or content that I want to study in depth, I will choose to mark it first. The purpose is to ensure a complete reading experience. Otherwise, if I am often distracted to study other things during the reading process, I may not be able to establish the correlation of the book content well.
3. Quiz # Ok, at this time I have finished reading a chapter, it is time to test my familiarity with the chapter.
At this time, I will use NotebookLM to create questions based on the content of the chapter. I will then actually do the questions to see if there are any misconceptions or unfamiliar parts.
If so, I will figure out the unfamiliar parts.
4. Deep Dive # In this stage, I already have a certain familiarity with the content of the book, it is time to deal with the content marked in the second stage.
I will pick out the marked content one by one and conduct in-depth research, discussion, and even implementation.
5. Output # After the previous steps, I should be very familiar with the content of the chapter at this time. It’s time to start the final integration and output it as an article.
In the process of outputting, I may find that I can’t explain it very clearly. This is another opportunity to review or figure it out.
Conclusion # I should execute this strategy for a while next, and I will share any insights and discoveries with you later XD

In recent years, “waking up early” seems to have become synonymous with successful people.
Many KOLs depict the beauty of waking up early in their videos, and numerous books studying successful people point out that one of their common traits is rising early.
However, is waking up early really that good? Is it suitable for everyone?
I have tried waking up early many times in the past, but this year I finally discovered: I am really not suited for waking up early.
The Benefits of Waking Up Early # Whether in books or videos, when explaining the benefits of waking up early, the following points are invariably mentioned:
Least Disturbance in the Morning # Indeed, if it’s early enough, others haven’t even woken up yet. But relatively speaking, if it’s late enough at night, you won’t be disturbed either.
Moreover, not everyone can really go to bed very early.
For example, I really like Muay Thai, and most Muay Thai classes are in the evening. Even if I wanted to switch to the morning, I couldn’t.
So if I were to wake up early, I would have to give up my hobby, switch to morning exercise, and train myself to get up even earlier.
Morning is When Thinking is Clearest # When you just wake up, you haven’t been exposed to the various noises of life yet, so this is when your concentration is strongest.
And because you just woke up, you have good energy.
But for me, it’s not like that. Night is when my thinking is clearest.
I don’t know why, but normally, my energy curve climbs slowly from the moment I wake up, and then there’s a moment when it suddenly drops, which is when I should go to sleep.
It sounds incredible, but roughly 10 PM to 1 AM is my peak energy time.
In addition, the noise in life is not just from the current day; yesterday’s noise can also have an effect. Unless you can leave all troubles from before today behind as soon as you wake up, but the reality is that it’s impossible.
Morning Exercise Hormones… # Some people say that exercising in the morning releases hormones, so you will be energetic blah blah blah (please forgive me for never really understanding this part).
My personal experience after trying many times is: Zero.
My energy didn’t improve; instead, I felt even sleepier after exercising.
And my athletic performance wasn’t good either; I felt groggy while exercising.
I didn’t sleep better at night either; insomnia was still insomnia.
What Matters is What You Do When You Wake Up Early # Many people say that you need to set a goal for waking up early, set something to do, so that you don’t wake up early and achieve no growth at all.
But after my own experiments, starting work immediately after waking up is the most efficient.
Why? As mentioned earlier, I am groggy in the morning, so it is really hard to have the willpower to do difficult things.
Most of the time, I just scroll through my phone, do some housework, and then it’s time for work. So what’s the point of me waking up early?
Some people might say: “Then your willpower is not enough.”
I agree 100% with this, but for the same things, if I put them at night, I have the motivation to do them.
In addition, work has a forced wake-up effect for me because I can’t escape work; I just have to deal with things.
However, I can start with a simple review in the morning, or do simple tasks first, to slowly wake up my brain.
Conclusion # Actually, looking back at the periods when I grew the fastest, none of them were because of waking up early. On the contrary, when I was growing fast, I usually went to sleep at 1 or 2 AM.
So this year I decided to analyze it and decided not to follow this “early rising success philosophy” anymore, and accept my own physiology and habits.
I hope this article can provide some reference for you who are also trapped by the idea of waking up early 😂

This article was translated by AI. If you find any errors, please feel free to email me at jk29666338@gmail.com 🙏. The content of this article references Gipi’s “How to Report Progress Well” course. Interested readers are welcome to take the course~ In the previous articles, we discussed the value of progress reporting and the consequences of not knowing how to report.
This article aims to explore: How should progress reporting be done? When is it appropriate to report? How to gauge the frequency?
When Should You Report Progress? # As a beginner in progress reporting, I might have a question:
So under what circumstances do I need to report progress?
A common answer is: during regular meetings.
Every department will more or less have Standup Meetings or weekly meetings. You can share the difficulties you encountered, what problems were solved, and what risks were seen during the regular meeting.
I think this method is very suitable for beginners because there is no need to make a special appointment with the supervisor, and other colleagues in the company can also know.
But you also have to be careful. The function of regular meetings is usually to synchronize progress. If too much time is spent sharing the details of personal tasks, others may be somewhat impatient.
And if we report some situations, the supervisor usually needs to make a decision. If everyone speaks at the meeting, the supervisor has to make many decisions at the meeting without time to collect more information or think, which may also cause discomfort to the supervisor.
So a more recommended direction of thinking is: Start from the manager’s personality and anticipate when they want to hear a report.
The Reporting Matrix of Psychological Safety and Trust # Everyone has a different level of psychological concern about risks. Some people are more optimistic, while others are more worrisome.
And this level of concern about risk is everyone’s psychological safety.
This kind of psychological safety is often something we cannot change. It is a set of values developed based on all his past experiences.
So when facing the supervisor’s psychological safety, we can only observe and adopt different strategies.
Another factor is trust, which is whether the supervisor can safely hand over tasks to employees.
When first joining a company, trust is usually low, but it can be accumulated slowly over time.
And the key to accumulation happens to be “progress reporting”.
So how do we know when to report progress through psychological safety and trust?
You can refer to the following figure:
Low Trust: High Frequency Reporting, Ask for Decisions # When the supervisor doesn’t trust you yet, you must report daily and ask for instructions on everything, big or small, and let the supervisor make decisions to accumulate trust.
Psychological safety is not a key determinant here, after all, psychological safety takes time to observe.
High Trust + Low Psychological Safety: Daily Sync, Align Together # When your results are slowly showing, and the supervisor affirms your ability and reporting ability, you can slowly change to this mode.
However, although the supervisor trusts you, he himself is easily anxious.
So you still need “simple daily synchronization” to reassure him. You can handle matters within your authority and inform him afterwards, but you need to align immediately when encountering changes.
High Trust + High Psychological Safety: Weekly Sync, Autonomous Decisions # This is the ideal state. Just report “weekly”, decide for yourself within your authority, and make suggestions for matters outside your authority for the supervisor’s reference.
Structure of Progress Reporting # Ok, we already know when to report work, but how exactly should we report it? Is there a structure that is easier for beginners to get started with?
First, we need to determine whether the current situation is as expected, or if it is actually not as expected (e.g., delays, technical difficulties).
On Track / As Expected # If things are going well, then simply synchronize the current results, explain the tasks for the next stage, and propose potential risks and preparation measures currently seen.
If things are going well because of your efforts, you can add whether you have resolved any issues in the process.
Off Track / Not As Expected # No one celebrates Chinese New Year every day; projects will always have times when they explode.
Of course, no one wants the project to explode, but if it really happens, you can change your mindset.
“Not as expected” is often a good opportunity to perform. Standing up when things are not as expected, eliminating the problem, and showing a responsible attitude will make others impressed with you.
The focus of progress reporting when “not as expected” is to show how to close the gap.
When reporting, you can refer to the following structure:
Gap Analysis: How much is the specific difference? How large is the impact scope? Cause Explanation: Why did it happen? Actions Taken: What has been done to stop the bleeding or remedy? Results and Expectations: What are the results after the remedy? When is it expected to catch up with the progress? Next Steps and Help Needed: What other risks are there? What resources are needed? Through the above structure, you can clearly let the supervisor know that you not only fully understand the gap, but have also formulated a plan and taken action. Instead of waiting for him to find out before dealing with it. “Trust” in you will instantly rise a lot.
I want to remind you again here that the focus of reporting when not as expected lies in how to eliminate the gap.
We must have three basic attitudes towards gaps:
First, Outcome First. No need to spend a lot of time finding someone to blame, explaining details, or explaining why the gap occurred.
Next, show the action and determination to try to catch up with the gap, rather than just explaining the gap.
Finally, think from a global perspective. Even if the gap is caught up this week, is it possible that the project will still be delayed?
Conclusion # In this article, we delved into when to report progress and the structure of progress reporting.
In the next article, we will start to explore common mistakes in progress reporting and things to pay attention to.

This article was translated by AI. If you find any errors, please feel free to email me at jk29666338@gmail.com 🙏. The content of this article references Gipi’s “How to Report Progress Well” course. Interested readers are welcome to take the course~ After reading the case in the previous article, we can probably gather that progress reporting is an important tool.
But I am used to carefully considering necessity, risks, costs, and benefits before doing anything.
After all, time is precious and should be spent on truly important things.
So this article mainly wants to explore:
The push factor of not reporting progress: The pain points of not reporting progress The pull factor of progress reporting: The benefits of progress reporting What Problems Arise from Lack of Progress Reporting # Usually, if there is a lack of progress reporting, you will encounter the following three dilemmas:
Falling into the Cycle of “Only Toil, No Credit” # Working hard and solving problems, but because it wasn’t shown at the right time, performance is not seen.
Never think that if you work hard and make everything go smoothly, the supervisor will see it all.
Just like I said in the previous article, if you only report results, the supervisor will only see the results, and won’t know how much bitterness lies behind this result.
Loss of Opportunities and Credit Being Harvested # Despite having strong abilities and a good attitude, promotions or good opportunities are always taken by others; even the results of one’s own hard work are claimed by other colleagues to invite credit because information was not synchronized in time.
This situation often occurs when what you do is a small part of the whole project. Because it is a small part, you don’t particularly want to report it.
And when the entire project is completed, usually the PM or technical lead is responsible for reporting on the project, and the boss/manager/colleagues from other departments won’t see your contribution.
Isolated and Helpless, Lacking Resources # When encountering difficulties, because no distress signal was sent through the reporting mechanism, no one reached out to help, and the boss couldn’t see your needs.
What’s worse is if the project is delayed because of this, and others need to help clean up the mess, affecting your reputation in the workplace.
The Three Core Values of Progress Reporting # I wonder what everyone thinks the meaning of progress reporting is?
At first I thought: “Oh, well, the company wants me to speak, so I’ll just say something briefly.”
I didn’t think about why the company wants us to do progress reporting, and the value it can bring if done well.
Of course, briefly saying what you are doing is also a kind of progress reporting. But it wastes the benefits that could come later.
I believe that a more ideal way is to treat progress reporting as an important tool for “Managing Up”, and its purpose lies not only in formal updates, but in achieving the following three strategic goals:
Establishing Consensus and Cognitive Alignment # Progress reporting can eliminate information gaps.
For example: Is what is currently being done in line with the supervisor’s expectations for this project? Is there any misunderstanding of the requirements? Is it on schedule?
Through reporting, both parties can reach a consensus on the current situation and requirements: the supervisor can quickly detect if something is wrong and make adjustments; and the employee can also avoid doing work in vain.
I have a painful experience with this.
During the execution of a project, I spent a lot of time implementing a complex algorithm.
I spent several days and finally implemented it. After demoing it to the PM, he said: “Oh, actually it doesn’t need to be this complex.”
I could only tearfully revert several days of hard work…
As a “Display of Work Results” # This is a “defensive” strategy.
Through daily and frequent synchronization, record your inputs, problems encountered, and the solution process.
When the supervisor already knows the process, it is difficult for others to harvest your results, and your contribution will not be underestimated.
Conversely, if you are used to only speaking up when you have achieved big results, it is very likely that you will be slowly harvested by others during the process.
I believe everyone has silently thought while listening to a supervisor’s report: “You talk big, but this project wouldn’t have gone so smoothly without me.”
I have also met kind-hearted people who would proactively give credit to others in meetings, for example: “This went so smoothly thanks to xxx’s help.”
Of course, you should be grateful when meeting such people, and if there is a chance, you can also become such a person yourself XD.
But unfortunately, there are not many such people, so it is best to rely on yourself to claim credit.
In addition, I believe that progress reporting essentially helps us build our resume content.
If you consistently report progress and document it, you will be able to easily answer questions about what problems you helped the company solve when looking for your next job.
As an “Opportunity to Get Assistance” # This is one of the most important functions of reporting —— “Avoiding Surprises”.
No one likes the feeling of the unknown, especially the feeling of “my house is on fire, but I’m the last to know”, which makes people feel extremely uncomfortable.
And when supervisors are afraid that employees have information leakage, a situation of “micromanagement” arises.
So when a project is about to go wrong, reporting early and explaining the solutions already attempted allows the supervisor to be mentally prepared and intervene to coordinate resources.
This makes the supervisor a partner in solving problems, rather than a blamer who is notified of failure at the end.
Over time, the supervisor can also feel more at ease believing that the employee will tell him about risks, he doesn’t need to do everything himself, and naturally will grant the employee more authority.
And the employee also gets more freedom and won’t be managed on everything.
The Three Levels of Progress Reporting # After reading the content above, I believe everyone should be able to realize that the ultimate goal of progress reporting is to create trust.
But in reality, to what extent do we need to do it? Is there anything we can focus on first as an indicator?
After all, wanting to get so many benefits from the start of progress reporting seems a bit unrealistic.
To answer this question, we can slightly divide progress reporting into three levels:
Creating a Sense of Security # As mentioned above, no one likes the feeling of “unknown”. “Unknown” makes people fearful and insecure.
Supervisors usually have supervisors above them, and bosses have board members above them. Supervisors also need to report to these big shots.
You can imagine that one of the supervisor’s demons is worrying that he can’t answer questions asked by these higher-ups.
So the primary task of progress is to provide enough information to let the supervisor grasp the current situation, especially the risk part, to avoid him feeling frustrated because he doesn’t know anything when facing his superiors.
Creating Consensus # Confirm through reporting that both parties have a consistent imagination of progress and direction, avoiding the tragedy of “I think it’s 90% done, but the supervisor thinks it’s still far off”.
Creating Value # This is the highest level, the purpose is “to be seen”.
Showcase work results and contributions through reporting, avoid silent dedication being ignored, or credit being harvested.
Conclusion # I believe that after reading this article, everyone can fully understand why “progress reporting” is so important.
Everyone might as well recall, in the past when you were doing work reporting, did you simply view it as a “routine duty”, or an “important tool”?
As for how to do progress reporting? When to report? What to pay attention to when reporting? We will leave that for future articles XD.

Recently, I inexplicably wanted to find a mobile game to play, so I looked around.
I’m not a hardcore gamer; I play mostly for leisure.
My expectations for a mobile game are roughly:
Exquisite 3D modeling: I quite like watching beautiful characters running around on the map. Not too brain-burning: I hope it’s action-oriented, without too many strategic elements. Can play happily without spending too much: No explanation needed XD. After clarifying my needs, I played “Genshin Impact” for a bit.
Actually, I had contact with it during university, and later quit and returned two or three times.
I think “Genshin Impact” is an excellent game, with diverse gameplay, and the story/music/art are all very good.
But “Genshin Impact” has a few pain points for me:
Gacha pressure (spending pressure): A team has four characters. If the strength of all four characters needs to be online, it’s actually quite stressful. And there’s a chance to lose the 50/50 when pulling for signature weapons… QQ Repetitive modeling: “Genshin Impact” characters all use a few fixed underlying models, and then different skins are put on the outer layer. I feel a bit fatigued looking at them after a while, feeling that every character looks about the same QQ. Elemental reactions: This is the core combat mechanism of “Genshin Impact”, but I find it so complicated XD. The deepest impression is that I spent a lot of money before to pull for Raiden Shogun and Furina’s constellations and signature weapons, but after pulling them and fighting bosses, I found it seemed to make no difference…
Are there other options? # Due to previous experiences, although I returned to “Genshin Impact”, I knew I would probably quit again soon.
So I started thinking if there were other options.
In between, I also downloaded the recently popular “Chaos Dream” (卡厄斯夢境) to experience it. The gameplay was quite good, but unfortunately, I don’t like card games XD.
Looking around, apart from the few games released by HoYoverse, “Wuthering Waves” had the highest acclaim. Then I saw a new character “Chisaki” (千咲) released recently, which I thought was quite nice.
So I thought I’d give “Wuthering Waves” a chance.
Starting Wuthering Waves # My first impression of “Wuthering Waves” was extremely poor, because I briefly joined when it first launched.
But that tutorial segment was really… I didn’t know what it was doing. I deleted the game directly afterwards.
But after two years, I found a few things:
Combat impact is great: For a mobile game, I think it’s not easy to achieve this. Many thoughtful little designs: For example, you can automatically teleport to the teleport point closest to the target, automatically fill in materials when upgrade points are insufficient… etc. Music, art, and animation significantly improved: Compared to the launch, the character ultimate animations are now super gorgeous. Some of the music really gives me goosebumps. There is a Mac version!!!: I don’t have a PC or game console myself, so being able to play on a Mac is just too enjoyable. Lower spending pressure than “Genshin Impact”: Includes only three characters in a team, lower pity count, weapon banner doesn’t lose 50/50, and constellation improvements are noticeable. Part of the story can be skipped: I don’t like being forced to stop and watch the story while playing games. “Genshin Impact” has no skip mechanism, while “Wuthering Waves” allows skipping parts of it. Doesn’t have to be very brain-burning: The combat mechanism of Wuthering Waves is also quite complicated, but not wanting to study it doesn’t mean you’ll be doing chip damage. Don’t know how long I can play # In the early stages of playing, I set a limit: I won’t spend money until I pull a five-star.
Because if I can’t even pull one for free, then I think it’s too painful.
However, around the seventh day of playing, the first five-star came out. I decisively made the first top-up double + small monthly card XD.
But there are still some small shortcomings currently:
Character materials gated by story: The materials for my current character require the story to be very far ahead, and I can’t fight for them in advance. It’s a bit painful 😭 iPhone/iPad tends to overheat: I use iPhone 15 Pro and iPad Pro, and they get very hot after about half an hour QQ. But overall I am satisfied ~ hope this game can accompany me for a while ~

This article was translated by AI. If you find any errors, please feel free to email me at jk29666338@gmail.com 🙏. Before getting to the main topic, I want to share a personal story of mine.
The first one happened during my university days. We had a class where we had to build a software project.
The teacher required us to give a group progress report every week. And to prevent anyone from slacking off, the teacher would grade each person individually during every report.
In that project, I mainly played the role of Product Manager. That is, I was mainly responsible for managing requirements and delivery, and I also had to ensure that UI/UX and engineers could work well together.
At that time, I felt that the PM’s work didn’t seem to have much to report. After all, the final output relied on engineers and UI/UX. In this role of coordination and requirement management, my traces wouldn’t be visible in the final result.
So during the weekly regular reports, I would just breeze through with a few sentences, trying to leave as much time as possible for other team members.
Later, after one of the reports, the teaching assistant secretly pulled me aside and said:
“I know you did a lot of things. You might want to try to say a bit more when you report.” The TA paused for a moment, then continued: “Otherwise, the teacher thinks that the work was done by Team Member A, but I know that you are actually the one who did the most.”
Honestly, I didn’t care about grades myself, but I felt it was unfair to other team members if someone who didn’t do work got a higher grade.
That was the first time I felt the importance of progress reporting. Even though I did more work, the credit was all taken by someone else entirely.
Later, when I entered the workplace, the company had meetings similar to progress reports every week/day. I also mainly just roughly talked about what tasks I did in the previous cycle, what tasks I am doing now, and when I expect to finish them.
It took less than 15 seconds to finish talking, very brief.
And during a 1 on 1, my supervisor told me:
“I think your technical skills are at a Senior level, because whatever task I give you now, you can probably get it done.”
“However, I still can’t 100% entrust tasks to you, the reason is that your ability to proactively report is a bit weak.”
“I know you are working, but perhaps you can speak up during every report, so that others will know, and you will have a better chance of promotion.”
I thought back a bit, and indeed, in the past, I would only choose to speak up when I encountered problems I couldn’t solve myself.
As for those I had already solved, or those I didn’t think were very important, I wouldn’t mention them specifically.
From the supervisor’s perspective, although he saw the result, he didn’t know what I considered during the process, what trade-offs I made, so he wouldn’t know what risks were actually hidden in this result that seemed to meet requirements.
And for me personally, if I only focused on delivering results, the supervisor wouldn’t know how many difficulties I encountered and how many problems I solved during the process.
These words woke me up and made me determined that I couldn’t continue like this.
So, I started on the journey of “improving the quality of work reporting”.
Reflection Questions # Before formally starting the content, I want to invite everyone to think with me:
In the workplace, exactly what kind of person is most likely to get promotion opportunities and be highly valued?
Is it strong professional skills? Is it managing up? Is it connections? Is it looks?
Of course, everyone’s life and career goals are different; not everyone wants to be promoted or highly valued.
But I think we can also think about it from another angle:
In the workplace, how can you ensure you don’t get disgusted by others? (e.g. framed, credit stolen, passing the buck)
In the last article of this series, I will reveal my answer after thinking about it, and I welcome everyone to see if your answer is the same as mine after reading this series XD.

I feel that this adjustment, firstly, gives me breathing room, so I don’t feel guilty for not working hard.
Secondly, it allows me to better distinguish between work and life. Otherwise, I used to have the feeling of “I can do it on the weekend anyway”, which actually led to a lack of focus.
I recommend everyone take a walk at the Science and Technology Museum if you have the chance~
